content.jointProblem: What mechanisms cause cracking at AutomVoj’s painted mild-steel conveyor welds after prolonged operation at 2–6 °C, and could changes to welding procedure, filler material or joint geometry reduce the damage? The first experiment would combine examination of the failed sections with matched room-temperature and chilled cyclic-load tests on representative joints, using measured service loads and temperature–moisture histories to test whether environmental exposure changes crack initiation or growth.

rationale.text: Erić has directly relevant experimental experience investigating the interaction of thermal cycling and mechanical fatigue in welded structural steel.

sources.quote: Four loading programmes were applied: isothermal fatigue at 20 °C, isothermal fatigue at −30 °C, in-phase thermo-mechanical fatigue (TMF), and out-of-phase TMF

rationale.text: He has experience turning measured industrial load and temperature histories into welded-structure fatigue assessments, supporting a service-informed rather than workshop-only investigation.

sources.quote: Rainflow-counted stress spectra and simultaneous temperature records were used to construct a combined loading environment for assessment.

rationale.text: His work combines weld residual-stress measurements with thermal–mechanical simulation, providing methods to investigate whether fabrication-induced stresses contribute to cracking.

sources.quote: Residual stresses in as-welded and post-weld heat-treated (PWHT) T-joint specimens of S460M low-alloy steel were measured by hole-drilling with strain-gauge rosettes
compared with sequentially coupled thermal–mechanical FE simulations.

rationale.text: His group routinely uses fatigue-testing equipment and a climate chamber, offering a relevant experimental basis for addressing AutomVoj’s testing gap.

sources.quote: The group routinely uses servo-hydraulic fatigue testing machines, a climate chamber capable of reaching −60 °C

constraints.text: Test specimens and any proposed modifications must represent the actual painted mild-steel hollow-section joints, particularly the crossmember-to-stringer connections.

sources.quote: Our conveyor frames are welded from mild steel hollow section and painted for corrosion resistance before delivery.
we are seeing weld joint cracking at the main crossmember-to-stringer connections

constraints.text: The investigation must distinguish actual chilled-service exposure from the room-temperature baseline and test the suspected thermal, moisture and vibration contributions rather than assume them.

sources.quote: We test frames under load at room temperature and they pass without any problem.
Our suspicion is that the combination of thermal cycling, condensation, and the vibration load from loaded belts

constraints.text: The initial failure analysis must work with the available site documentation and two retained failed sections; specimen allocation must be agreed before destructive examination.

sources.quote: We have photos and measurements of the cracked joints from site visits, and we still have two of the failed sections in storage.

constraints.text: Combined chilled cyclic-load testing requires external laboratory access, and extended campaigns must be scheduled around the researcher’s shared equipment.

sources.quote: We do not currently have the equipment or know-how to test at low temperatures under cyclic load.
Erić's climate chamber and servo-hydraulic machine are shared with two other research groups; scheduling access for extended test campaigns requires advance coordination.

constraints.text: Company engineering effort must be explicitly reserved alongside live delivery work because there is no dedicated R&D team.

sources.quote: We have no dedicated R&D department
our chief engineer and two senior automation engineers who allocate time between live projects and improvement work.

risks: Transfer is unvalidated: the cited studies largely concern specified structural-steel grades, different joint geometries and substantially colder conditions. They do not establish the cause of cracking in painted mild-steel hollow sections at 2–6 °C; the first matched-joint experiment must test this transfer.
Condensation and coating-related corrosion may be important, but the supplied evidence does not establish the researcher’s corrosion-fatigue expertise or the laboratory’s humidity-control capability.
Actual vibration spectra, thermal transients, material grade and fabrication variability are not supplied. An unrepresentative accelerated test could reproduce a different failure mechanism.
Two retained failed sections may limit destructive analysis and may not represent all 14 warranty failures.
Researcher availability, equipment booking dates, project budget, customer-site access and the required completion date remain unknown; these could prevent a sufficiently representative campaign.
Failure after approximately 18 months creates a validation-time risk: accelerated laboratory results may not demonstrate equivalent service life or elimination of warranty failures.
questions: What are the exact steel grade, wall thickness, joint drawings, filler specification, welding parameters, inspection records and coating system, and are comparable unfailed joints available?
Can the failed sections and site records be released for examination, and which destructive analyses may be performed?
Can customer sites provide access for strain or vibration measurements and temperature–humidity logging, including loading changes, shutdowns and washdown or condensation events?
Can the laboratory reproduce 2–6 °C cyclic loading with controlled moisture exposure on representative joints, and what fixtures, specimen dimensions or external corrosion expertise would be needed?
What are Erić’s availability and the shared equipment booking windows, and who at AutomVoj can commit engineering and fabrication time?
What budget, deadline and staged acceptance criteria should govern mechanism identification, comparison of modifications and subsequent service validation?
